**Yes. We can build yyot as one logical assistant per workspace, with private DM sessions and shared channel sessions. A permanent Hermes instance per user isn’t inherently required.**

Each user’s DM gives them a private conversation. The backend must preserve that privacy when retrieving memory, accessing accounts, and executing tools.

For v1, I’d treat **each Slack workspace as a tenant**:

| Conversation | Context available to that conversation |
|---|---|
| Workspace A → Sahan’s DM | Sahan’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → Nishank’s DM | Nishank’s private history and authorized resources |
| Workspace A → `#project` | That channel’s shared discussions, documents, and approved results |
| Workspace A → private `#finance` | Context restricted to that channel’s audience |
| Workspace B → any conversation | Workspace B’s authorized context, isolated from A |

**The architecture would have five responsibilities:**

1. **Route by verified identity.** Every request carries its workspace, sender, and conversation. These come from authenticated Slack events.
2. **Load the appropriate conversation.** DMs load personal context; channels and threads load shared context. A channel conversation cannot retrieve somebody’s DM history.
3. **Keep persistent data scoped.** Memory, files, browser sessions, and credentials retain their owner or audience. Switching conversations must also switch which resources are accessible.
4. **Run tools with limited access.** Shared infrastructure coordinates requests. Browser and generated-code work runs in isolated environments with access only to the authorized owner’s resources. These workers can start when needed.
5. **Deliver to the correct audience.** Private account observations stay in a private execution session. Only owner-approved content enters the channel’s shared conversation.

For example, Sahan could ask in `#project` to prepare a report using his private account. yyot handles the account work privately, sends him the result in a DM, and publishes the content he approves. Nishank can contribute requirements without acquiring Sahan’s account access.

**When Prateek joins:** joining Workspace A gives him access according to its channel membership, without exposing other users’ DMs or accounts. Installing yyot in his own Workspace B creates another tenant with separate context and resources.

Hermes already supports separate DM sessions and shared channel/thread sessions. However, its profile routing does **not** implement end-user authorization, and profiles do not sandbox filesystem access. Those protections still require yyot integration. [Session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions), [authorization boundary](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals), [sandboxing distinction](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/profiles/#profiles-vs-workspaces-vs-sandboxing).

**This would revise our design to shared agent infrastructure, separate conversation state, and isolated task execution.** It reduces the need for permanent personal runtimes, while making correctly scoped memory and tools essential.

| Tenant | Hermes deployment | Conversations it serves |
|---|---|---|
| Your workspace | Instance A | Sahan’s DM, Nishank’s DM, shared channels/threads |
| Another company’s workspace | Instance B | That company’s DMs and channels/threads |

Within each instance:

- **DM history and personal resources stay user-scoped.**
- **Channel context is shared with that channel’s audience.**
- **Browser/file tasks run with isolated, owner-authorized access.**

The instances can share physical cloud infrastructure while having separate runtime environments and storage.

**Tenant isolation separates companies. yyot’s authorization and context handling still have to protect individual users within each company.**

**It can. A separate Hermes instance per tenant was an isolation option I suggested, not a technical requirement.**

We could run **one shared Hermes-based service serving many tenants**, with separate sessions and permissions:

| Shared | Kept separate |
|---|---|
| Agent software and orchestration | Each tenant’s data and configuration |
| Model service | Each conversation’s history and memory |
| Hosting infrastructure | Users’ credentials, browser sessions, and private files |

For every request, yyot would identify the tenant, user, and conversation, then load **only the context and tools that request is authorized to access**. Generated code would execute in an isolated worker without access to the shared service’s databases or other users’ resources.

The distinction is **one shared agent engine versus one shared conversation and unrestricted access to everyone’s data**.

The tradeoff: fewer deployments, but more responsibility in yyot’s authorization, memory retrieval, and execution controls. Hermes’s routing alone doesn’t implement those permissions. [Hermes authorization boundary](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/multiplexing-gateway/#non-goals)

**One shared service is a viable architecture. We haven’t established a reason that yyot requires an instance per tenant.**

**Yes. With the browser integration included, yyot v1 could be mostly configuring, hosting, and validating Hermes. I overstated how much custom engineering we necessarily need.**

Hermes already documents browser automation, encrypted credential storage, secret-free browser filling, automatic TOTP generation, and credential removal. We should reuse those. [Browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/).

And the assignment explicitly says:

> “We care more about one smooth, working experience than the amount of code.”

It permits third-party components. A solution built largely from Hermes is consistent with that brief. :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Downloads/Zonko Labs Engineering Assignment.pdf" purpose="source"}

**What we’re responsible for delivering is the complete reviewer experience:**

1. **Connect and manage access from Slack.** Can Sahan securely provide credentials, complete verification, and remove access without touching our server or using Hermes’s desktop app?
2. **Keep users’ access correctly separated.** Do our chosen profiles, sessions, and permissions protect private accounts while allowing shared channel conversations?
3. **Demonstrate reliable completion.** Does it reuse access in fresh browsers, recover from interruptions, and verify results across different websites?

Those are **checks to perform**, not three custom systems we should automatically build. Existing configuration or plugins may satisfy them. Hermes already provides substantial profile routing and session functionality. [Profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes).

Full SaaS tenancy and team collaboration are extensions we discussed beyond the original assignment’s central browser-and-credentials brief.

**Our contribution may ultimately be deployment, configuration, a few integration fixes, and convincing execution evidence. If upstream Hermes passes every required flow, there’s no reason to manufacture additional code.**
